story.title: The Fermi Award
story.goalShort: I want to accept the award without groveling or sulking, and say one true thing to the President.
story.goalFull: I want to accept the Fermi Award at the White House without groveling or sulking, and say one true thing to the President while the room watches.

facts: Johnson went ahead with the ceremony as scheduled, in the Cabinet Room.
I stood next to him, and by one account I looked like a figure of stone, gray and rigid, while Kitty was a study in joy.
With Peter and Toni looking on, Johnson said a few words and handed me a medal, a plaque and a check for $50,000.
In my acceptance speech I said that Thomas Jefferson often wrote of the brotherly spirit of science.
I said, "We have not, I know, always given evidence of that brotherly spirit of science."

I said it wasn't for lack of common scientific interests, but because we are engaged in the great enterprise of our time, testing whether men can both preserve and enlarge life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness, and live without war as the great arbiter of history.
I turned to Johnson and said, "I think it is just possible, Mr. President, that it has taken some charity and some courage for you to make this award today."
I added, "That would seem to me a good augury for all our futures."
Johnson answered graciously, calling Kitty the "lady who shares honors with you today, Mrs. Oppenheimer," and then, to laughter, said, "You may observe she got hold of the check!"
Teller was in the audience, and everyone watched with mounting tension as we came face to face.
With Kitty standing stone-faced beside me, I grinned and shook his hand.
A Time magazine photographer caught the moment.
Afterwards Mrs. Kennedy sent word that she wanted to see me in her private quarters.
Kitty and I went upstairs and she greeted us.
She said she wanted me to know just how much her late husband had wanted to give me this award.
